bp: The ordinary problem behind this tutorial is that web knowledge does not sit still. A search system or question-answering system may find a page that talks about the right person, product, law, election, disease, or company, but the answer can still be wrong if the page describes an old state of the world. For temporal information retrieval and temporal question answering, relevance has two parts: whether the information is about the user's need, and whether it is valid for the time being asked about. A query such as who leads an organization, what rule applied during a past year, or how a fact changed after an event cannot be handled as timeless text matching. The tutorial serves the builders of information access systems that must retrieve, interpret, and reason over evolving web knowledge. Its purpose is to connect older temporal search ideas with modern large language models and retrieval-aided answer generation.
wh: The hard part is that time is not just another keyword. A document can mention the right topic while mixing facts from different dates, publishing dates, event dates, update dates, and periods of validity. A system must decide which clock matters. The page date may tell when text was posted, while the sentence may describe something that was true years earlier, and the user's question may ask about the present or a specific past interval. Large language models add another tension: they can write fluent answers, but their stored knowledge may be stale, and retrieved passages may conflict because the web preserves old and new claims side by side. Classical search ranking mostly asks which documents are topically useful. Temporal retrieval asks a stricter question: useful when? The system must adapt as knowledge changes, without treating every old source as false or every recent source as correct.
naive: A smart beginner would first take a normal search or question-answering system and add date filters. For current questions, show newer pages; for historical questions, search for the year in the query; for answers, feed the top pages into a language model and ask it to respond. This helps only in clean cases. It fails when the needed time is hidden inside the text rather than in the page metadata, when an old article remains the best evidence for a historical question, when a new page repeats outdated information, or when several sources describe different valid periods. It also fails when the model answers from memory instead of checking whether the retrieved evidence matches the user's intended time.
ap: The central move is to make time a first-class part of information access rather than a cleanup step after retrieval. The tutorial frames temporal information retrieval and temporal question answering as linked tasks: first find information that is both topically relevant and time-valid, then reason over it so the answer respects when facts held. It traces a path from explicit rules and probability-based methods to neural models, transformer architectures, and large language models, but the underlying move stays the same. The system must represent temporal clues, compare them with the time asked about, and adjust retrieval or generation when knowledge evolves. In retrieval-aided generation, that means the language model should not merely receive documents; it should receive evidence whose time conditions have been considered, so the produced answer is grounded in the right slice of the changing web.
mech: The mechanism begins with a user need: a query or question that may ask about now, a past moment, a future-facing trend, or an event sequence. The system reads the words for topical intent, but it also looks for temporal intent: explicit dates, words like current or former, event references, and implied timing. It then examines candidate web evidence. Each candidate has content and some temporal signals, such as publication time, update time, dates mentioned in the text, or spans during which a claim appears valid. A temporal retrieval component scores candidates by two kinds of fit: whether they discuss the right subject and whether their time aligns with the question. Earlier systems might do this with hand-written rules or probability estimates over date evidence. Modern systems may use neural models and transformer-based language models, where a transformer means a model that repeatedly lets words inspect other words in context, so a date expression can influence how the surrounding claim is understood. For temporal question answering, the selected evidence is then organized so the answer can distinguish old from current, before from after, and valid during from merely published during. In retrieval-aided generation, outside documents are brought to the language model at answer time; the temporal version adds a gate that asks whether those documents are timely evidence before their facts shape the answer.
math: The main mathematical idea is ranking under an added constraint. Ranking means giving each candidate a score for how well it should be shown before the others. In ordinary search, the score mostly measures topical closeness between query and document. Here the score must combine topical closeness with temporal fit, so a document can lose rank even if its words match well, because its claim belongs to the wrong period. Probability also enters naturally because temporal evidence is incomplete. A date in a document is not always the validity date of the claim, so the system estimates which interpretation is most plausible from repeated clues. Sequence reasoning matters because web knowledge evolves: facts appear, expire, are corrected, and get reused. A model must treat information as an ordered stream rather than a static pile. Retrieval-aided generation adds a second mathematical object: evidence selection before generation. The system chooses a small set of passages from a large collection, balancing completeness against the risk of stale or conflicting evidence. The tradeoff is speed and coverage versus temporal precision. Too strict a time filter misses useful evidence; too loose a filter lets old truth contaminate the answer.
dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of search, question answering, ranking, sequences, and retrieval-aided generation. The repo's ranking concept already captures the key shift: retrieved information must be ordered by topical relevance and by validity over time, not just by word match. It also connects to the retrieval-augmented family, where many papers ask how a language model should use outside evidence instead of relying only on stored memory. The temporal version adds a special failure mode: the evidence may be real but no longer valid, or valid only for a past interval. Nearby time-series papers in the same batch, such as online forecasting and time series generation, also treat order as essential, but their object is numeric or behavioral sequences. This tutorial applies the same deeper pressure to web knowledge: the order of events and updates changes what counts as a correct answer.
ww: It works because many mistakes in information access come from collapsing different times into one undifferentiated fact store. If the system separates topical relevance from temporal validity, it has more ways to reject misleading evidence. A page about the right entity can be kept for a historical question and demoted for a current one. A recent page can still be questioned if it repeats a claim whose real validity period has ended. A language model can be useful after retrieval because it can synthesize evidence and explain relationships, but it needs the retrieval stage to supply time-appropriate material and it needs reasoning that notices before-and-after structure. The tutorial's unified view is valuable because older rule-based and probability-based temporal methods solved parts of this problem before large language models arrived. Modern systems can inherit that discipline: do not ask only whether text sounds relevant; ask when the claim is supposed to hold and whether the evidence supports that time.
po: The payoff is a clearer design map for systems that answer questions over an evolving web. The tutorial promises participants a comprehensive overview of temporal retrieval and temporal question answering, from older rule-based and probabilistic approaches through neural methods, transformer models, temporal retrieval-aided generation, and temporal reasoning over changing knowledge. That buys practical guidance for building search and answer systems that are less likely to treat stale information as current truth. It also gives the field a shared vocabulary for open challenges: how to model time, how to adapt when knowledge changes, and how to make language-model answers respect temporal evidence.
limits: Because this is a tutorial abstract, it does not claim a new dataset, algorithm, or measured performance result. Its value is synthesis and education, so the abstract cannot prove that any particular temporal retrieval or answer-generation method solves the problem in deployment. The approach assumes temporal signals can be found or inferred from documents, queries, and retrieved evidence; when dates are missing, ambiguous, contradictory, or intentionally manipulated, the system can still be wrong. It also assumes that large language models can be guided by retrieved evidence rather than overriding it with stale memory. The abstract names open challenges, so temporal precision, adaptation, and trustworthy reasoning remain unfinished engineering and scientific problems.
